HJOB-CTX-G1.title: Tallowmarket research notes before the onsite
HJOB-CTX-G1.text:
TALLOWMARKET - MY RESEARCH NOTES BEFORE THE ONSITE
Last updated Sunday night. Sources: their engineering blog, the Series C press release, two podcast interviews, and a coffee chat with a former engineer (Wes Adeyemi, left in 2025).

COMPANY BASICS
- Founded in 2019 in Boulder by Renata Obi (CEO, used to own a restaurant) and Cal Whitford (CTO). HQ moved to Denver LoDo in 2022.
- Series C of $64M in February 2026, led by Harlan Ridge Ventures. The press release says the money goes to "payments infrastructure and expanding into the Pacific Northwest."
- About 140 people, roughly 55 in engineering (matches the job posting).

PRODUCTS I SHOULD MENTION
- Fieldpay (launched spring 2025): growers can get paid 2 business days after delivery instead of waiting on the restaurant's 21-day terms. Tallowmarket fronts the money and holds the restaurant's payment in escrow. This is why the Payments & Ledger group exists in its current form.
- Tallow Terms (pilot): net-30 credit for restaurants, currently piloting with about 300 restaurants in Colorado only. Renata said on the Supply Side podcast that Tallow Terms is "the riskiest thing we've ever built" because Tallowmarket carries the credit risk.

ENGINEERING - WHAT THE BLOG SAYS
- "Why we built Harrow" (post by Staff Engineer Maren Dahlquist, 2024): they moved from a single balances table updated in place to a double-entry ledger. Main reasons: they could not explain balance drift to Finance, and refunds were being applied twice when a webhook retried.
- Temporal adopted in 2023 for long-running payout workflows.
- A 2025 postmortem post: the nightly settlement batch overran by about 3 hours one night in November because of lock contention on the payouts table after a big Thanksgiving week. The fix was splitting the batch by grower region and moving to SKIP LOCKED workers. The post ends with "we still don't have good backpressure when volume spikes" - so it is still an open problem.

WHAT WES TOLD ME (coffee chat, take with a grain of salt)
- On-call was heavy in 2024; he thinks it got better after the Harrow cutover.
- Design docs really are the culture. Reviews are async, with a 48-hour comment window.
- The Payments team is 8 engineers. He said the manager is great at shielding the team but is stretched thin.

HOW MY BACKGROUND MAPS (talking points)
- Settlement reconciliation at Larkspur (312 to 41 monthly mismatches) is the closest thing I have to ledger work. Be honest: I have not built a double-entry ledger.
- Dockhand's transactional outbox is the same idea as avoiding the double-applied refunds in the Harrow post.
- Sparrowhawk (idempotency keys on PostgreSQL advisory locks) is directly relevant to webhook retries.
- Partitioning load_events by month is relevant to their volume growing from 400k to 1.5M entries per day.

QUESTIONS I WANT TO ASK
1. What does backpressure on the settlement batch look like today, a year after the November overrun?
2. How is the Tallow Terms credit risk modeled in the ledger - separate accounts, or a separate system?
3. What would success look like for this hire in the first 90 days?

THINGS I DON'T KNOW YET
- Whether the Pacific Northwest expansion changes the team structure.
- Who the hiring manager is (the recruiter never said).

PI-A:JD.title: the job description the user is targeting
PI-A:JD.text:
SENIOR BACKEND ENGINEER, PAYMENTS & LEDGER
Tallowmarket, Inc. | Denver, CO

ABOUT TALLOWMARKET
Tallowmarket is a B2B marketplace where independent restaurants buy directly from regional farms and ranches. Our Payments & Ledger group moves about $1.1B a year through escrowed payouts to more than 6,500 growers. We are a team of 140 people, about 55 of them in engineering. Our backend is Go on PostgreSQL, with Kafka between services and Temporal for long-running payment workflows.

WHAT YOU WILL DO
- Own services in the money path: escrow holds, split payouts to growers, refunds and chargebacks.
- Design and evolve Harrow, our double-entry ledger built on PostgreSQL, as volume grows from 400,000 to a projected 1.5 million ledger entries per day.
- Improve the reliability of the nightly settlement batch that runs at 02:00 Mountain Time and must finish before banks open.
- Lead technical design reviews and mentor mid-level engineers on the team.
- Join the on-call rotation, currently one week in six.
- Partner with Finance and Risk on reconciliation and audit requirements.

WHAT YOU BRING
- 5+ years of professional backend experience in Go, Java or Kotlin.
- Deep PostgreSQL knowledge: indexing, locking, isolation levels, and safe online migrations.
- Experience with event-driven systems (Kafka, Kinesis or similar) and idempotent processing.
- A track record of leading multi-engineer projects from design doc to launch.
- Clear written communication; we make most decisions in design docs.

NICE TO HAVE
- Prior work on a double-entry ledger or a payments platform.
- Experience reducing PCI DSS scope.
- Stripe Connect or Adyen for Platforms integration experience.
- Experience with Temporal or another durable workflow engine.

WORK ARRANGEMENT
Hybrid: in our Denver LoDo office Tuesday through Thursday; Monday and Friday are flexible. Relocation assistance is available for candidates moving to the Denver metro area.

COMPENSATION
Base salary band: $172,000 - $208,000 USD, plus equity and a 6% 401(k) match. This role is leveled at L5 (Senior).

INTERVIEW PROCESS
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), a 60-minute ledger design exercise, a Go coding session, and a values conversation with our Director of Engineering, Imani Castellanos.

Tallowmarket is an equal opportunity employer.

items.question: Why's that?
conversation: INTERVIEWER (heard): So from what you've seen of us, what do you think is the hardest problem our payments team is dealing with right now?

NATIVELY: The hardest thing I'd guess is what happens when volume spikes. The 2025 postmortem on the nightly settlement batch said the fix was splitting by grower region and moving to SKIP LOCKED workers, but it ends by saying there still isn't good backpressure when volume spikes. That reads like the open problem, and it's close to what I work on now, settlement reconciliation and event pipelines at high volume.
items.answer: The postmortem itself doesn't say why backpressure is still open, so this is my read rather than something the post states. Splitting by grower region and moving to SKIP LOCKED workers fixes the lock contention, but it doesn't cap how much work arrives at once. items.question: Tell me about Dockhand. Why a transactional outbox instead of just publishing to Kafka directly from the service?
items.answer:
Dockhand is a Kafka event pipeline I designed at Larkspur Freight. It handles about 2.3 million shipment status events a day, and it uses a transactional outbox table to avoid duplicate writes.

The reason for the outbox is that writing to the database and publishing to Kafka are two separate systems. If you publish straight from the service, a crash between the DB commit and the Kafka send means the event is lost, or a retry means it goes out twice. The outbox puts the event in the same transaction as the state change, so a relay can publish it afterward and it stays consistent.

items.question: How comfortable are you writing Go? And have you run Kafka in production?
items.answer: Go isn't on my list yet. My main languages are Python, Rust and Bash, and most of my work has been Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus, so I'd be picking Go up on the job. Kafka I haven't run in production either. What I have run is a four-node k3s cluster with Flux GitOps, Loki and Grafana, so the operational side of running a broker is familiar ground.

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Let's talk numbers. What base salary are you looking for?
items.answer: The band for this role is **$172,000 to $208,000** base, plus equity and the 401(k) match, so I'd be looking at the upper half of that given the scope of the money-path work. What I'd want to understand is how you level within the band and what the equity looks like, since that shapes the whole picture. What range were you thinking for someone coming in at L5?

items.role: USER: the job candidate. OTHER PARTY: the interviewer / recruiter. Natively: what the candidate says, in first person. Résumé/JD (if in evidence) are the candidate's own.
items.question: Alright, let's get into it. How do you usually work with product managers and designers day to day, like when a spec is still fuzzy?
conversation: INTERVIEWER: Sorry, give me one second, my dog just decided the mail carrier is a threat.
USER (spoken): No worries at all, mine does the exact same thing.
INTERVIEWER: Ha. Did you get hit by the snow out there? We got almost a foot overnight.
USER (spoken): Just a dusting here, but the roads were still a mess this morning.
items.answer: When a spec is still fuzzy, I try to get in the room early rather than wait for something polished. I ask what problem we're actually solving and what the smallest version looks like, then we sketch options together and I flag the tradeoffs I see on the technical side. That way we're deciding together instead of me just building what's written down.
